documents.title: AAGBI recommendations for standards of monitoring during anaesthesia and recovery

chunks.content: Introduction Cesarean section (CS) is a common operation performed worldwide with approximately 18.5 million procedures being performed annually. Recent global data estimate that nearly 20% of pregnant women give birth via cesarean delivery ( ). The CS rate has large variations in different countries and regions, ranging from merely 5% in South Sudan to 58.9% in the Dominican Republic ( ). In the United States, the cesarean delivery rate is estimated to be almost a third of all births, with over 1.2 million procedures performed every year ( ). In China, the CS rate was much higher than the ideal rate recommended by the WHO. More notably, the rate of cesarean delivery on maternal request, the main indication for unnecessary CS, was also high with more than 28% ( ). In addition, international analysis shows that the CS rate has witnessed a steady increase and does not show signs of decrease over the past few decades ( ). Thus, the huge volume of cesarean deliveries and increasing CS rate has an incremental burden on healthcare systems, leading to higher bed occupancy and financial pressures on the patients and health facilities ( , ). While the decrease in the CS rate is crucial, it is also apparent that CS will continue to be a necessary procedure for obstetricians. Therefore, it is not surprising that growing interest will focus on introducing improved perioperative care for CS. In particular, enhanced recovery care is an effective way to improving the clinical and health system benefits of CS, which have been shown to promote rehabilitation and earlier discharge ( ). Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) is a multimodal and multidisciplinary approach to optimizing the perioperative management and outcomes ( ). The core tenets of the ERAS have been outlined previously and are positioned along the entire surgical care continuum, aiming to alleviate the surgical stress response, promote functional recovery, and achieve rapid recovery ( , ). ERAS has been widely implemented in multiple surgical disciplines including colorectal, urologic, hepatobiliary, and gynecologic surgery ( , ). However, the implementation of ERAS in the obstetric field has lagged compared to other surgical subspecialties ( ). Since the ERAS concept was proposed in the field of obstetrics surgery, there has been a slower embrace of ERAS application to CS. Currently, some maternity centers are endeavoring to use ERAS protocol in their clinical practice, showing some advantages over conventional care in CS ( ). In the last 5 years, several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies were published to evaluate the superiority and feasibility of ERAS for CS, providing better evidence linking ERAS implementation and maternal outcomes including a reduction in hospital stay, lower incidence of complications, and quicker functional recovery ( – ). However, currently no meta-analysis specifically addresses the impact of ERAS on maternal outcomes among women undergoing CS. In this context, quantifying summary evidence involving the comparative effect of ERAS on maternal outcomes is warranted. In this study, we perform a systematic review and meta-analysis to qualitatively and quantitatively assess the clinical efficacy and safety of ERAS protocols for CS, compared with conventional care. Importantly, the overall effect estimated from the existing literature will be helpful in guiding decisions of ERAS practice. Methods Literature Search and Selection Criteria This systematic review and meta-analysis were performed in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. A systematic search of the databases of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Embase was conducted to identify relevant studies. The last search was run on October 19, 2020, and language was limited to English. The following medical subject heading terms and free-text terms individually or in all possible combinations are as follows: “Enhanced recovery after surgery” OR “Accelerated rehabilitation” OR “ERAS” OR “Fast track” OR “Early Recovery” OR “Enhanced Recovery” AND “cesarean” OR “cesarean” OR “cesarean delivery” OR “cesarean section” OR “cesarean section.” In addition, we reviewed the full-text articles designated for inclusion and manually checked the references of the retrieved articles and previous reviews to identify additional eligible studies. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies meeting the inclusion criteria will be enrolled: (1) participants: patients underwent elective or emergency cesarean section; (2) intervention: ERAS management protocol was proposed in the study; (3) controls: the conventional care protocol was used for patients receiving CS; (4) outcomes: including at least one main outcome of interests; and (5) design: RCTs or observational studies (prospective or retrospective cohort studies). The exclusion criteria were the following: (I) full text of the article was not available; (II) the outcomes of interest were lacking or impossible to calculate or extrapolate; (III) the types of article were not original articles such as reviews, meta-analyses, comments, case reports, letters to the editor, or protocols; and (IV) republished study. in the study; (3) controls: the conventional care protocol was used for patients receiving CS; (4) outcomes: including at least one main outcome of interests; and (5) design: RCTs or observational studies (prospective or retrospective cohort studies). The exclusion criteria were the following: (I) full text of the article was not available; (II) the outcomes of interest were lacking or impossible to calculate or extrapolate; (III) the types of article were not original articles such as reviews, meta-analyses, comments, case reports, letters to the editor, or protocols; and (IV) republished study. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment Two authors (X. M. and K. C.) screened the titles and abstracts of the initial search results, extracted the data, and assessed for risk of bias independently. Disagreements were resolved by group consensus. Clinical data were extracted from qualified studies and subsequently analyzed. The following information was extracted from the included study: first author, year of publication, country, study design, number of patients enrolled, and patient characteristics (age). The primary outcome was length of hospital stay (LOS). Secondary outcomes were postoperative complications, readmission rate, postoperative pain score, postoperative opioid use, and cost of hospitalization. The quality of RCTs was assessed by the Cochrane risk of bias tool including selection biases, performance biases, detection biases, attrition biases, reporting biases, and other biases ( ). Observational studies were evaluated using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS), which included adequacy selection of cohort, comparability of studies, and outcome assessment. Statistical Analysis All statistical analyses were calculated by RevMan 5.3 software. The dichotomous data were performed as risk ratio (RR), and continuous variables were expressed as weighted mean differences (WMD) or standard mean differences (SMD). All results were performed with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Some data presented with median, and ranges or interquartile ranges were converted into mean and standard deviation using approaches described by Wan et al. ( – ). Initial analyses were assessed using the fixed-effect model. Heterogeneity was tested using I 2 and chi-squared tests. Heterogeneity was categorized as low ( I 2 < 50%), moderate ( I 2 = 50–75%), and high ( I 2 > 75%); I 2 > 50% indicates significant heterogeneity ( ). For outcomes detected with significant heterogeneity, sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the results by the sequential omission of individual studies. The sensitivity analyses adopting a random-effect model was also conducted to test the stability of pooled estimates. Publication bias was estimated by the use of funnel plots. Results Characteristics and Quality of Eligible Studies A total of 186 records were retrieved from the initial literature search. After excluding duplicates (60 records), we identified 126 records to screen titles and abstracts. One hundred fourteen records were removed for various reasons based on the titles and abstracts (reviews, meta-analyses, correction, editorial, response, or supplements, etc.). Subsequently, the remaining 12 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and two were excluded for unextractable useful outcomes data. Finally, 10 studies were included in the meta-analysis ( – , – ). The selection process is presented in . summarizes the characteristics of the included studies. All studies were published from 2019 to 2020. In total, this meta-analysis involved 16,391 patients, of which 7,595 received ERAS protocols and 8,796 received conventional care. Of the included studies, four were RCTs and six were cohort studies. Among the 10 studies, seven were conducted in America, one in Africa, and two in Asia. Risk of bias for RCTs is shown in . Attrition bias, selection bias, detection bias, reporting bias, and other bias were reported adequately in most studies. However, the performance bias was high risk among all the selected studies, because the participants could not be blinded due to the counseling and education of ERAS protocols. The quality assessment of observational studies based on the NOS is presented in . Only one study achieved the maximum of nine stars. Of the remaining five studies, all achieved eight stars. The majority of bias was found in the comparability of cohorts, because most of the studies lacked a modified control for some important factors. Outcome Measures Length of Hospital Stay A total of six studies with appropriate data reported the LOS. The forest plot indicated that the ERAS protocol was associated with a shorter LOS as compared to the conventional group (WMD −7.47 h, 95% CI: −8.36 to −6.59 h, p < 0.00001), with significant heterogeneity ( I 2 = 98%, p < 0.00001) ( ). ERAS protocol was associated with a shorter LOS as compared to the conventional group (WMD −7.47 h, 95% CI: −8.36 to −6.59 h, p < 0.00001), with significant heterogeneity ( I 2 = 98%, p < 0.00001) ( ). The sensitivity analysis showed that the original analysis was not changed by omitting one study in each time, ranging from −6.24 (95% CI, −7.15 to −5.34; I 2 = 97%) to −12.14 (95% CI, −13.31 to −10.96; I 2 = 98%). Furthermore, the result of the random-effect model (WMD −11.38; 95% CI −19.52 to −3.24; p < 0.00001) was in agreement with the result of the primary analysis, demonstrating that the result was reasonably stable. Postoperative Complications Four studies reported the postoperative complications. The forest plot showed that the rate of postoperative complications was lower in the ERAS group (RR: 0.50, 95% CI: 0.37 to 0.68, p < 0.00001, fixed-effect model), without significant heterogeneity ( I 2 = 45%, p = 0.14) ( ). In addition, further exclusion of any single study did not materially alter the overall combined RR. Readmission Rate Seven studies reported the readmission rate involving 15,353 participants. The forest plot showed that ERAS decreased the readmission rate in comparison with the conventional group (RR: 0.72, 95% CI: 0.55–0.94, p = 0.02, fixed-effect model). The reported heterogeneity was judged to be moderate ( I 2 = 64%, p = 0.01). However, the pooled data based on the random-effect model identified no significant difference in the readmission rate between the two groups (RR: 0.86, 95% CI 0.48–1.54, p = 0.62) ( ). The sensitivity analysis also confirmed the study by Hedderson et al. which showed a significant effect on heterogeneity ( ). The heterogeneity decreased ( I 2 = 16%) after removal, as shown in the study by Hedderson et al., and new results also indicated that no significant difference was found in terms of readmission rate (RR: 1.07, 95% CI 0.74–1.53, p = 0.73, I 2 = 16%). Postoperative Pain Score and Opioid Use A total of four studies reported a postoperative pain score involving 1,686 participants. The postoperative pain score was significantly lower in patients receiving ERAS than those receiving conventional care (WMD: −1.23, 95% CI: −1.32 to −1.15, p < 0.00001, fixed-effect model), with significant heterogeneity ( I 2 = 98%, P < 0.00001) ( ). Therefore, the sensitivity analysis showed that the result was stable and no study had a significant impact on the overall results. Also, the random-effect model was applied to this result and showed a similar significant effect (WMD: −0.88, 95% CI: −1.69 to −0.07, p = 0.03). Postoperative opioid use was reported in four studies; pooled results showed that ERAS protocols significantly reduced the postoperative opioid use (SMD: −0.46, 95% CI −0.58 to −0.34, p < 0.00001), with moderate heterogeneity ( I 2 = 66%, p = 0.03) ( ). Application of a random-effect model revealed a similar significant reduction in opioid use (SMD: −0.44, 95% CI −0.65 to −0.23, p < 0.0001, I 2 = 66%). Cost of Hospitalization Only three studies with the appropriate data reported cost of hospitalization involving 10,374 participants. The estimated SMD for the meta-analysis was −0.54 (95% CI −0.63 to −0.45, p < 0.00001), indicating a reduction in the hospital cost for the ERAS group as compared with the control group ( ). The I 2 statistic indicated that there was a significant heterogeneity ( I 2 = 98%). Application of the random-effect model did not affect the result (SMD −0.97, 95% CI: −1.78 to −0.16, p = 0.02; I 2 = 98%, p < 0.00001). Due to the limited included studies, we did not conduct sensitivity analysis by the leave-one-out method for this result. Publication Bias and Sensitivity Analysis Finally, because all pooled analyses include <10 comparative studies fr analysis quantitatively, publication bias detection could not be examined. To evaluate the robustness of the association results, sensitivity analysis using leave-one-out and random-effect modeling was performed to test the stability of the pooled data. Most of the sensitivity analysis results remained stable, indicating the consistency of the pooled results including LOS, postoperative complication, postoperative pain score, postoperative opioid use, and cost of hospitalization. Only the sensitivity analysis for readmission rate showed inconsistent results; we adopted the results of the sensitivity analysis as the final effect. It has disrupted the traditional principles of surgical therapeutics and medical understanding with its superior clinical, social, and scientific effects ( ). Discussion ERAS is an innovative rehabilitation model applied to the perioperative period in the recent years. It has disrupted the traditional principles of surgical therapeutics and medical understanding with its superior clinical, social, and scientific effects ( ). However, the safety and efficacy of ERAS in CS remain controversial. Therefore, we conduct this study to add more granular data regarding the clinical outcomes following ERAS implementation in CS. This is the first meta-analysis including comparative studies of ERAS protocol and conventional care to evaluate the maternal outcomes. Our findings showed that ERAS protocols resulted in favorable outcomes in CS as indicated by reduced postoperative complications, lower hospital costs, and shorter LOS without increasing the need for readmission. It is also worth mentioning that the ERAS protocols reduce the patients' postoperative pain, while not aggravating the opioid use. The sensitivity analyses confirmed the consistency of the results. LOS is an important index in assessing the benefits of postoperative recovery and has been traditionally one of the key outcomes of ERAS. From the results of the meta-analysis, we found that shorter LOS was presented in the ERAS group. Although the reduction of LOS was <1 day in the analysis, the decreased LOS represented the faster recovery and earlier discharge with clinical significance. Some evidence has documented that early discharge after CS can improve maternal–neonatal bonding and maternal satisfaction coupled with financial savings ( ). Moreover, there was also evidence showing that even day-one or day-two discharge appears to be safe and acceptable in low-risk patients undergoing cesarean delivery ( ). In the future, the ongoing evaluation of maternal outcomes, neonatal factors, and readmission rates is useful in better confirming optimal discharge times and LOS ( , ). Readmission rate is another concern in clinical practice, because higher rate of readmission is a potential barrier for ERAS implementation and negatively affects the life quality of patients ( , ). Our results did not show that the application of ERAS increases the readmission rate, indicating the safety of applying ERAS in CS. Even our primary results showed that ERAS could decrease the readmission rate; the sensitivity analysis finally confirmed that the readmission rate has no significant difference between two groups. Admittedly, postoperative complication is also a major concern in postoperative care, because postoperative complications hindered early discharge and potentially increased the healthcare costs and utilization of hospital resources. Our results suggested that ERAS protocol reduced the rate of postoperative complications. This result was consistent with implementation of ERAS in other non-obstetric patients, demonstrating the superiority of ERAS in improvement for postoperative complications. There are several reasons addressing ERAS implementation with such striking clinical results. Firstly, detailed preoperative education and psychological counseling from ERAS protocols will be helpful in easing the psychological pressure and improving patient compliance to ERAS protocol ( ). Secondly, ERAS protocols reduce fasting time and increase carbohydrate intake to relieve the stress of hunger and anxiety before CS, decreasing the insulin resistance and the loss of nutrition in the postoperative period ( ). Third, ERAS protocols advocate early removal of urinary catheter and mobilization, thereby decreasing the risk of urinary tract infections and postoperative venous thromboembolism (VTE) ( – ). Fourth, standardized care practices, standardization of the use of prophylactic antibiotics, and early mobilization in ERAS have supported significant reductions in postoperative infections such as surgical site infections, lung infection, and urinary tract infection ( ). Fifth, excellent analgesia, intraoperative warming, and early postoperative oral feeding are all essential to accelerating recovery via maintaining body homeostasis, promoting discharge earlier, and reducing postoperative complications ( ). More importantly, ERAS works improve most parts of the perioperative process and achieve additive benefits beyond the individual modifications ( ). Postoperative pain management has been an essential issue related to postoperative recovery in patients receiving CS ( , ). While opioid use is an important aspect of postoperative pain control in patients undergoing CS, excessive opioid use brings many side effects affecting maternal and newborn health ( , ). Additionally, postpartum pain and opioid-related side effects may influence the maternal–fetal bonding and maternal recovery ( ). In this regard, to test the evidence considering the connections between implementation of ERAS in CS and postoperative pain and opioid use is meaningful. Our pooled analysis supported that ERAS implementation improves the postoperative pain scores and lowers the opioid consumption in CS. Interestingly, Hedderson et al. showed that women undergoing CS and receiving ERAS protocol had higher acceptable pain scores for all postoperative days ( ). Our pooled analysis supported that ERAS implementation improves the postoperative pain scores and lowers the opioid consumption in CS. Interestingly, Hedderson et al. showed that women undergoing CS and receiving ERAS protocol had higher acceptable pain scores for all postoperative days ( ). We speculate that beneficial effects to pain control and opioid consumption arising from ERAS may be multifactorial. An important aspect of ERAS is the multimodal analgesia scheme, which has shown to alleviate concerns regarding opioid use, reduce pain scores, and enhance patient comfort ( ). In particular, the multimodal approach to opioid-sparing pain control adopted in ERAS also brought other benefits such as earlier recovery of gastrointestinal function, early ambulation, fetal protection, and reduced risk of maternal opioid abuse ( , ). Importantly, the decrease in postoperative pain score does not come at the price of increased opioid consumption. Therefore, it could be inferred that pain relief mainly benefited from the effect of ERAS protocol implementation rather than excessive use of opioids. Our results highlight the importance of ERAS for post-CS pain management. In addition, other factors may influence pain relief including anxiety and anticipated pain ( ). Improving these concerns before surgery may reduce pain perception and increase maternal satisfaction. Perioperative education and psychological counseling of ERAS, anticipated pain severity, and pain control strategies obviously reduce anxiety and set realistic expectations, positively influencing the opioid consumption and pain scores ( , ). Taken together, the use of the multimodal analgesia approach, characteristic of ERAS, might be a viable strategy for lowering opioid use and pain score postoperatively. Economic burden is an unignored factor considered in the clinical practice of ERAS. Our results showed that the cost of hospitalization was significantly lower in the ERAS group than in the control group, suggesting that implementing ERAS protocol in CS is cost-effective. However, due to the limited studies assessing data of hospital cost, more high-quality trials were needed to determine the true cost-effectiveness of ERAS. We speculate that the saving of hospital costs mainly benefits from shorter hospital stay, reduced drugs, and lower complication rate, although ERAS contains the use of diverse medical care modalities and treatment approaches ( ). The present encouraging results would greatly promote the implementation of ERAS protocols in maternity units. In addition to aforementioned advantages of ERAS implementation in CS, it may have other potential benefits such as improving patient satisfaction and increasing the breastfeeding rate. However, data involving these specific effects of ERAS are limited and unclear. Only a few investigations demonstrated that ERAS may improve patient satisfaction, breastfeeding, and mother–child bonding. Hopefully, more studies will be conducted to evaluate these beneficial effects of ERAS, further exploring the effects referring to neonate outcome, postpartum depression, and service efficiency. Despite our careful work on the currently available evidence, several limitations should be interpreted in this meta-analysis. Firstly, only four RCTs were included in the present study and some outcomes mainly derived from cohort studies rather than RCTs; thus, the results may have been influenced by information bias, selection bias, and detection bias, as well as confounding bias. Secondly, none of the RCTs featured blinding, potentially leading to performance bias and measurement bias. It is noted that the blinding for the ERAS protocol is not feasible in clinical practice. Thirdly, the ERAS protocol elements in each study may be different slightly, leading to inescapable heterogeneity. Conclusions Our results showed that protocols implementing ERAS in CS could shorten LOS and hospital cost and reduce the incidence of complications, postoperative pain score, and opioid use, but could not increase the rates of readmission. Our data add to the evidence supporting that ERAS protocols applied to CS are feasible, effective, and safe. However, limited to the quantity and quality of the studies and their potential heterogeneity, further large and randomized controlled studies should be undertaken to confirm the present findings. documents.title: AAGBI guidelines peri-operative care of the elderly

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION “Low-value care” describes health care services which either do not change patient outcomes or cause more harm than good. Routine preoperative testing (e.g. electrocardiograms, chest x-rays, blood and urine tests, etc.) in most patients undergoing low-risk surgery constitutes low-value care. - Numerous studies including several systematic reviews and metanalyses have demonstrated such testing does not prevent adverse events or improve outcomes and can cause harm via invasive care cascades (i.e. follow-up invasive testing), surgical delays, and financial waste for both patients and healthcare systems. - For example, one study of patients without known cardiac disease undergoing cataract surgery showed that a quarter of patients who underwent unnecessary electrocardiograms (EKGs) ultimately experienced more than four cascade events including follow-up testing and hospitalizations. Unnecessary preoperative testing and resultant cascade events are estimated to cost the US healthcare system $18 billion annually, and patients experience financial toxicity in the form of additional out-of-pocket expenses and missed days of work. Other studies have demonstrated harm secondary to surgical delay caused by unnecessary testing in the form of prolonged hospital stays and patient falls. , As a result, multiple professional societies recommend against routine preoperative testing. For example, the international Choosing Wisely campaign recommends against preoperative tests before low- and intermediate-risk surgeries. Additionally, the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines discourage routine testing for otherwise healthy patients. Despite these recommendations, unnecessary testing remains common with significant variation within and between hospital systems despite adjusting for patient risk. Hospital systems with high utilization of preoperative testing routinely test nearly 90% of patients, while low utilization hospital systems evaluate procedure-matched patients with testing approximately 20% of the time. Internal chart review data suggest the academic institution examined in this study falls into the top half of testing in the state, with 60% of patients receiving at least one preoperative test. Though about half of all patients across the state of Michigan receive at least one unnecessary test, de-implementation efforts have been limited. , - An early review of trends in de-implementation for seven Choosing Wisely campaigns found mixed results; some of the selected initiatives saw reduction in low-value care while others saw an increase, suggesting published recommendations alone are not enough to change practice. Clinicians are a clear source of variation between hospital systems, so we sought their perspectives to elucidate specific motivations behind overtesting. This study aimed to identify determinants of unnecessary preoperative testing across a diverse group of individuals to inform future de-implementation strategies targeting participant-identified barriers. We conducted observations and interviews at one institution with surgeons, anesthesiologists, nurses, and physician assistants at outpatient surgery centers and preoperative clinics and used narrative thematic analysis to evaluate interview transcripts. METHODS STUDY DESIGN To understand determinants of unnecessary preoperative testing, we investigated perceptions and experiences of those involved in daily practice as well as their organizational constraints through an ethnographic study. Focused ethnography is a qualitative methodology applied to studying specific problems or processes requiring in-depth, nuanced understanding of organizational cultures and contexts. We conducted direct observations, semi-structured interviews, and analysis of relevant artifacts at two preoperative clinics and one ambulatory surgery center within a single academic institution in order to capture preoperative processes in detail, from multiple perspectives. Artifacts included preoperative testing protocols, practice preference documents for individual surgeons, and case order forms within the electronic health record. Themes were identified using narrative analysis further described below. This study is reported according to the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) Checklist ( ). STUDY SITE The study was conducted at a single academic institution identified as a moderately high utilizer of preoperative testing compared to institutions across the state of Michigan (top 50% of testing based on internal chart review data). The academic institution has two freestanding ambulatory surgery centers and five preoperative evaluation clinics. Observations and interviews were conducted at one freestanding ambulatory surgery center and three preoperative evaluation clinics. We targeted clinics and an ambulatory surgery center performing three target low-risk operations based on prior work in this area (lumpectomy, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and inguinal hernia repair). The institution serves a relatively healthcare-dense geographic region and does not draw from a rural population for these low-risk operations. Patients undergoing surgery at this institution are first seen in outpatient surgical clinics for consultation with their surgeon. Most low-risk patients have a subsequent preoperative appointment in dedicated preoperative clinics with a Physician Assistant (PA). At this appointment, the preoperative history and physical is completed as well as any ordered laboratory testing and imaging. Appointments are conducted either virtually or in-person. Low-risk patients are not routinely evaluated by anesthesiologists as outpatients prior to the day of surgery. Internal data suggests preoperative testing is ordered more commonly by surgeons and preoperative PAs than by anesthesiologists. At this appointment, the preoperative history and physical is completed as well as any ordered laboratory testing and imaging. Appointments are conducted either virtually or in-person. Low-risk patients are not routinely evaluated by anesthesiologists as outpatients prior to the day of surgery. Internal data suggests preoperative testing is ordered more commonly by surgeons and preoperative PAs than by anesthesiologists. FRAMEWORK Data collection was organized by the Tailored Implementation for Chronic Diseases (TICD) framework ( ). The TICD is a consolidated checklist that describes factors influencing change in clinical practice. Determinants are subdivided into 7 domains, including (1) guideline factors, (2) physician and (3) patient-level factors, (4) professional interactions, (5) incentives and resources, (6) capacity for organizational change, and (7) other social, political or legal factors. - We used this framework to structure data collection through an interview guide, observation protocols, and structured field notes template. We employed deductive coding based on TICD determinants for barriers and facilitators of de-implementation to identify determinants of low-value pre-operative testing. ETHICS, CONSENT, AND PERMISSION This study was exempt from ongoing review by the University of Michigan institutional review board (IRBMEDHUM00224219). We received verbal consent before each interview and observation. Participants volunteered their time and were not financially compensated. PARTICIPANTS, RECRUITMENT, AND INTERVIEW PROCEDURES We defined healthy patients as those with American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class 1 (normal) or 2 (mild systemic disease) designation. We defined low-risk surgery by the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines plus operations with less than one percent risk of thirty-day serious adverse events. , Observations were conducted at two preoperative clinics and one ambulatory surgery center by three researchers trained in qualitative methodology (CR, CP, AV). We observed everyday workflows at all sites and engaged in conversation with informants in the natural setting where the behaviors of interest occurred. In this setting, we sought out conversations with additional informants and followed observation opportunities as the natural environment revealed both individuals and matters of interest. Key artifacts (namely, documents, order sets, and workflow diagrams) were photographed for later analysis. Participants at these sites were informed of the purpose and structure of the study and volunteered to be observed and/or interviewed. Structured notes were written within 72 hours of each day-long observation period. Several interviews were conducted onsite during observations. At the end of an observation period, key informants were invited to interview using a semi-structured interview guide. Interviews were recorded and transcribed as below. Other surgeons and primary physicians were recruited for interview via email. We used purposive sampling in order to obtain perspectives of potential informants who were absent or completing clinical duties during observation periods. The invitation email included a description of the study purpose, interview process, and analysis plan. Interviews were conducted either in-person or through video conferencing (Zoom Videocommunications) by two interviewers (CR and CP). Interviews were conducted according to an interview guide developed by the research team ( ). All interviews were recorded, transcribed verbatim, verified by one researcher (AV), and de-identified before analysis. ANALYTIC APPROACH Qualitative data from de-identified transcripts were analyzed thematically using MAXQDA 2022 (VERBI Software, Berlin, Germany). We developed a codebook using both deductive and inductive coding. Deductive codes were determined based on the interview guide and TICD framework prior to data analysis and assigned to excerpts reflective of those codes. Inductive codes were added based on site-specific contexts during data analysis. Transcripts were coded independently by four researchers (CR, CP, AV, and MB) and disagreements in coding were resolved through discussion via weekly meetings. We then conducted narrative thematic analysis by writing iterative, critically reflexive memos on coded data systematically. RESULTS Thirty individuals participated, including 8 surgeons, 5 anesthesiologists, 2 primary care providers (PCPs), 9 preoperative physician assistants (PAs), 2 certified registered nurse anesthetists, 3 nurses, and one medical assistant. Surgeons practiced surgical oncology (2), minimally invasive (5), and colorectal (1) specialties. Over seven hours of interview conversations were audio-recorded, transcribed, and coded. Mean interview length was 36 minutes (range: 6-41 minutes). Structured notes derived from over 15 hours of direct observation were analyzed. We identified three major themes via iterative narrative analysis. Exemplary data are reported in and . THEME 1: SHARED VALUES: SAFETY AND EVIDENCE-BASED MEDICINE Participants frequently named safety and evidence-based medicine as key tenets of the preoperative process, mapping to TICD Social, Political, and Legal factors. Many participants falsely believed routine preoperative testing improved patient safety by preventing adverse events. They believed routine testing may “catch that one in a thousand,” despite recognizing that most patients do not need testing most of the time (Participant 6). During observations, several clinicians acknowledged their patient may not have a clear indication for a given laboratory test, but explained they were ordering it anyway “to be safe” (Participant 10, 15). One preoperative PA stated testing was often performed “out of an abundance of caution” rather than to change management (Participant 6). Many individuals also viewed preoperative testing as a safeguard against medicolegal risk should an adverse event occur. One surgeon imagined an adverse event and subsequent lawsuit with prosecutors arguing “if someone gets hurt, no one cares that the surgeon tried to save $3 on a sodium” (Participant 10). Similarly, a surgeon reflected on the same sentiment by imagining four potential outcomes of a preoperative type and screen. In one instance, the surgeon orders the test, the patient loses no blood, and nothing happens. In another case, they order the test, the patient experiences massive hemorrhage, and they are glad they ordered it. In a third case, they do not order the test, the patient experiences massive hemorrhage, and the surgeon regrets not ordering it given patient safety risks. Finally, they do not order the test, the patient does not bleed, and no one notices anything. The surgeon explained appropriate, guideline-supported testing for a low-risk surgery is not memorable (Situation 4). In contrast, they felt providers are more likely to remember disaster scenarios (Situation 3), even if rare, and may adjust practice patterns to mitigate perceived risk (Situation 2). Thus, TICD social factors (a culture of prioritizing safety) and legal factors (mitigating perceived risk) together motivate a routine testing approach. In the same way that safety was a core value amongst participants, so, too, was the idea of evidence-based medicine. Participants across roles shared a commitment to the practice of clinical medicine based on updated data published in the scientific literature. Several providers stated that compelling evidence disseminated by a reliable source, such as a professional organization or a clinical department, would make them more comfortable ordering fewer preoperative tests. Ironically, these data and guidelines exist, but not all clinicians were aware of them (TICD Guideline Factors). As a result, some clinicians did not practice evidence-based medicine despite endorsing it as a value. Specifically, clinicians stated they would follow hypothetical guidelines without realizing such guidelines are already published. THEME 2: GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE Participants demonstrated variable knowledge of evidence-based guidelines supporting less testing (TICD Individual Health Professional Factors & Guideline Factors). Some clinicians demonstrated excellent knowledge of guidelines and harms regarding low-value testing with one participant noting the “published data show[s] a lot of these tests are unnecessary” (Participant 12). This group additionally claimed they avoided ordering routine preoperative tests in low-risk cases. We observed one clinician in this group actively deselecting default orders within an embedded order set in the Electronic Medical Record (EMR) to remove an unnecessary preoperative test from their orders. Furthermore, several embedded order sets and case order forms examined during artifact analysis automatically included unnecessary preoperative tests. Other clinicians shared they were unaware of the data but questioned their own practices during conversation, expressing that further guidance would be helpful. For example, one surgeon reflected on his practice of ordering routine preoperative type and screens, concluding: “I’m not sure why I order that. It’s exceedingly rare that you would need blood products at the beginning of the surgery, or even emergently in any way so I’m not sure why we order that at all” (Participant 11). These clinicians ordered tests out of habit but were open to changing practices if provided with supportive evidence. A third group was similarly unaware of contemporary guidelines yet persisted in the belief that routine preoperative testing was “useful to me” (Participant 9). Clinicians in this group emphasized perceived benefits of adverse event prevention, medicolegal risk reduction, and increased patient safety, while posing minimal harm. They disagreed there was significant utility in eliminating routine preoperative testing in even low-risk cases, mapping to TICD Individual Health Professional Factors: (Dis)Agreement with the Recommendation. Many individuals reported confusion around other clinicians’ desire for testing. Across disciplines, clinicians feared case cancellation on the day-of surgery and, as a result, reported ordering preoperative tests to meet perceived expectations of other providers despite themselves believing the tests were unnecessary. For example, one surgeon stated, “I think anesthesia wants labs” (Participant 11). Additionally, we observed confusion in preoperative holding areas between preoperative nurses, anesthesiologists, and surgeons regarding the need for preoperative EKGs. Despite being unsure which provider (if any) requested or needed the EKG, all clinicians moved forward with having the test done to minimize perceived risk of case delay. Completing the EKG was perceived as more time-efficient than initiating a discussion with all team members to obtain permission to omit the test (TICD Incentives and Resources). Anesthesiologists noted over-testing by surgeons but felt no incentive to initiate discussion to suggest process modifications or improvements, given nearly all cases proceeded as planned. PCPs and PAs were aware of unnecessary testing but felt that “just ordering the stupid EKG” was more efficient than initiating a communication channel with surgical or anesthetic teams to clarify the test’s necessity (TICD Incentives and Resources) (Participant 13). In preoperative evaluation clinics, we observed several PAs using internal records of individual surgeons’ historical preferences and ordering testing accordingly. Artifact review of preoperative clinic documents revealed individual surgeons’ guideline-discordant preferences were recorded and circulated to promote efficient patient throughput to surgery. These documents and other organizational strategies were used internally by preoperative PAs to ensure all patients of specific, individual attendings received preoperative testing regardless of the patients’ medical histories. Some PAs reported attempting to initiate discussion about the necessity of testing in the past but found the conversations time-prohibitive given “too many emails” (Participant 4). DISCUSSION All clinicians included in our study shared the common goal of bringing patients through surgery safely and efficiently. Clinicians ordered unnecessary preoperative testing for a variety of reasons including the misperception that routine testing increases patient safety, is free from harm, and mitigates medical and legal risk, in addition to attempting to meet perceived expectations of other providers. This practice was compounded by communication challenges across large, interdisciplinary teams in which ordering preoperative testing was easier than initiating discussions to obtain permission to omit them. Some clinicians also demonstrated gaps in knowledge of contemporary preoperative testing guidelines, with additional variation in the attitudes they expressed toward changing practices. Given surgeons, anesthesiologists, and other preoperative clinicians do not normally see downstream harm from low-value testing in their own routine practice, they perceive “no downside” to ordering the tests and are incentivized to act against practice recommendations (Structured Field Notes, Ambulatory Surgery Center). Game theory describes a systems-level conflict generated by independent decision-makers acting rationally within a system. , Individuals choose sensible actions given role-specific pressures, yet results are suboptimal when these decisions function within the broader system. In the perioperative space, clinicians share a common goal of bringing patients to the operating room safely and efficiently, yet they are incentivized to act against preoperative testing guidelines in the process. As a result, unnecessary testing is ordered to increase perceptions of efficiency and safety on the individual level while causing harm on the population level. At the level of the individual patient, any additional preoperative tests may well be the most efficient route to surgery for the clinician . Notably, this route is not more efficient for the patient, as the need for testing necessitates an in-person encounter while the preoperative evaluation may otherwise be completed virtually. Moreover, unnecessary preoperative tests have a major impact at the population level on cascade events, surgical delays, and financial cost for both patients and the healthcare system. , , - To facilitate effective de-implementation, individual incentives must be re-aligned to encourage practice in accordance with guidelines. In other words, we must restructure clinical systems to align patient-level preoperative testing practices with population-level goals. Interventions to decrease unnecessary preoperative testing must address determinants at the level of both individual clinician and hospital systems. On the level of the individual clinician, educational efforts should address the misperception that unnecessary preoperative testing is harmless by increasing understanding of cascade events, surgical delays, and associated risks (e.g. patient falls

In other words, we must restructure clinical systems to align patient-level preoperative testing practices with population-level goals. Interventions to decrease unnecessary preoperative testing must address determinants at the level of both individual clinician and hospital systems. On the level of the individual clinician, educational efforts should address the misperception that unnecessary preoperative testing is harmless by increasing understanding of cascade events, surgical delays, and associated risks (e.g. patient falls from delayed cataract surgery), as well as patient financial toxicity and overall healthcare costs. , - Individualized provider audit and feedback may highlight individual surgeon testing practices relative to both colleagues and guidelines and could provide internal motivation for change. Systems-level changes are also necessary to incentivize clinicians to act according to guidelines by making “the right choice” also the easiest one. For instance, preoperative order sets and practice advisories within the EMR should provide guideline-based recommendations during clinical encounters and not require clinicians to “un-check a box” to follow best practices. Existing evidence-based guidelines should be made uniform within institutions to eliminate the need for preoperative clinicians to change routine testing practices based on individual surgeon preference. Consensus guidelines may also streamline inter-provider communication by clarifying interdisciplinary needs and reducing testing ordered to meet perceived expectations of other clinicians. The subgroup of clinicians who disagreed with contemporary guidelines and insisted routine preoperative testing was useful may require more extensive interventions to elicit change, such as pay-for-performance initiatives. Interdisciplinary communication challenges and the pressure to practice efficiently are not unique to our institution. Strategies addressing these challenges are likely to improve workflow and guideline adherence across a range of practice settings. Prior work has estimated only 12% of variation in preoperative testing practices can be explained by facility-level factors, suggesting most variation comes from within an institution itself. Our analyses support this data, as a lack of protocolized preoperative testing practice may lend itself to the aforementioned interdisciplinary challenges. LIMITATIONS This qualitative study was conducted at one large academic institution. Most low-risk surgical patients at the institution visit a preoperative clinic staffed by PAs prior to surgery. Our results may not be generalizable to institutions with varied preoperative processes and non-academic institutions. However, it is likely that systems utilizing non-surgeon clinicians for preoperative evaluation (e.g., PCPs) would experience similar findings given evaluation by multiple clinicians creates clinical momentum for testing and produces the communication challenges discussed above. Our data illustrate systems-level pressures felt by a diverse group of individuals which may exist within other systems and could be targeted by similar de-implementation efforts. Future work in this area could benefit from ethnographic study at other sites, including hospital systems identified as low utilizers of preoperative testing, community hospitals, and others. Additionally, we did not evaluate subjects’ perspectives on the utility of individual preoperative tests, such as an EKG versus basic metabolic panel versus chest X-Ray. Future work should assess whether clinicians have reservations about de-implementing particular preoperative tests. However, given high rates of unnecessary testing of all types, we believe our study reveals important initial findings about the motivations behind such testing. CONCLUSION Despite recommendations against routine preoperative testing, the practice is common for a variety of reasons including perceived safety of patients and clinicians, fear of case cancellation and procedural delays, and conflict avoidance within interprofessional health systems. Our data demonstrate many clinicians would be amenable to evidence-based change, but that education alone will likely be insufficient to change practice patterns. Our findings suggest de-implementation may be more successful with emphasis on clinicians’ shared commitment to evidence-based medicine through broad educational efforts, consensus guidelines, and streamlined interdepartmental communication. By implementing systems-level changes to preoperative testing, health systems may alter the “game theory calculus” to incentivize clinicians to adhere to practice guidelines.
